title: Project Northstar automatic-merge decision
question: Should Project Northstar enable automatic merging for AI-generated dependency updates during the next four-week release cycle?
verdict: Do not enable automatic merging under the proposed rule for the next four-week cycle. The evidence supports considering a later, explicitly scoped rollout for low-risk patch updates, but the current rule includes protected surfaces and lacks provenance and rollback evidence.

nodes.label: Do not enable the current rule
nodes.text: Project Northstar should not enable automatic merging for AI-generated dependency updates under the currently proposed rule during the next four-week release cycle.

nodes.label: Reliability evidence is narrowly scoped
nodes.text: The observed reliability result supports only low-risk patch updates evaluated by the required checks, not the full set of updates the proposed rule would cover.

nodes.label: Generated recommendations are not auditable from their descriptions
nodes.text: Without signed provenance, a reviewer cannot verify from a generated pull-request description what model, prompt, or advisory produced its recommendation.

nodes.label: The rule covers protected surfaces
nodes.text: The proposed rule does not exclude packages with install scripts or updates touching authentication code.

nodes.label: Automation could reduce review delay
nodes.text: Routine patch-update review had a 31-hour median wait in the prior four-week cycle, so automatic merging could reduce that delay.

nodes.label: Rollback readiness is unmeasured
nodes.text: Whether an automatically merged bad dependency update can be rolled back quickly enough is unknown because no rollback drill or recovery-time measurement is recorded; a poor result could change the decision.

nodes.label: Controlled replay passed most low-risk patches
nodes.text: In a synthetic replay, 18 of 20 low-risk patch updates passed the complete test suite without manual edits, and required checks detected both failures before merge.

nodes.label: Replay excluded high-risk categories
nodes.text: The replay did not include major-version updates, packages with install scripts, or changes to authentication and authorization code.

nodes.label: No signed provenance for generated descriptions
nodes.text: The fixture has no signed provenance record for generated pull-request descriptions, so a reviewer cannot verify the model, prompt, or retrieved advisory from a description alone.

nodes.label: Proposed rule lacks key exclusions
nodes.text: The proposed rule currently excludes neither packages with install scripts nor updates that touch the authentication directory.

nodes.label: Routine patch review waits 31 hours
nodes.text: The synthetic team recorded a median wait of 31 hours for routine patch-update review during the previous four-week cycle.

nodes.label: No rollback drill or recovery measurement
nodes.text: No rollback drill has been recorded for an automatically merged dependency update, and the fixture contains no measurement of recovery time after a bad merge.

edges.note: The replay shows that required checks caught both observed failures in the tested low-risk patch population.
The excluded major, install-script, and authentication categories limit the replay's relevance to a broader automatic-merge rule.
Because reliability was demonstrated only for a narrower population, it does not justify enabling the current broader rule.
The absence of signed provenance directly prevents a reviewer from tracing a generated recommendation using its description alone.
An unauditable generated recommendation is a reason not to remove human review through the current automatic-merge rule.
The stated lack of exclusions directly establishes that the proposed rule covers install-script packages and authentication changes.
Including protected surfaces is a reason not to enable automatic merging under the rule as it currently stands.
The measured 31-hour median wait establishes a review-delay problem that automatic merging could reduce for routine patch updates.
A material opportunity to reduce routine patch-review delay is a reason in favor of enabling automatic merging, against the current no-enable position.
The absence of both a recorded rollback drill and recovery-time measurement establishes the stated rollback-readiness gap.
Without rollback evidence, the team cannot assess whether a bad automatic merge can be recovered within an acceptable time; that missing fact could change the decision.
